input.quote: Either Party may, without consent of the other Party, assign this Agreement in whole to (i) in the case of RevMed, its successor in interest or assignee or purchaser, as applicable, in the case of a Change of Control or (ii) in the case of Sanofi, its successor in interest or assignee or purchaser, as applicable, in connection with the sale of all or substantially all of its assets to which this Agreement relates, or in connection with a merger, acquisition or similar transaction.
input.rationale: The grant package clears the fallback and nearly all of the preferred checklist, so no redline is warranted. (1) Affiliates: Section 3.4(a) lets Sanofi "exercise its rights and perform its obligations under this Agreement by itself or through the engagement of any of its Affiliates without RevMed's consent," and Section 15.2(a)(i) permits assignment to any Sanofi Affiliate without consent — better than the fallback's "on written notice" condition, so no affiliate language needs adding. (2) Contractors: Section 3.4(c)(i) allows Sanofi to subcontract its Research, Development, Manufacture and Commercialization tasks to Third Parties "as Sanofi deems appropriate," with sublicensing through multiple tiers under Section 3.4(b). (3)/(4) Paid-up licence: Section 12.3(b) provides that on expiration the Section 3.1 licences "become fully paid up, royalty free, perpetual and irrevocable"; the Section 3.1 grant is not stated to be revocable at RevMed's discretion, so walk-away territory is not engaged. (5) Successor transfer: Section 15.2(a)(ii) permits Sanofi to assign the Agreement in whole to a successor in a merger, acquisition or similar transaction without RevMed's consent. The only preferred sub-element not fully met is that the royalty-bearing (term) licence can end on RevMed terminations beyond uncured material breach — insolvency (12.2(c)), Competing Product (12.2(d)) and cessation of development (12.2(e)) — but that is a negotiated collaboration construct outside the fallback checklist and is noted rather than flagged; those triggers are conditional and cure-based, not discretionary revocation.
